A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIKASA study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched despite renumbering, layout changes, and expanded evaluations.

before.justification: v1 Section 6.3 and Appendix D report original PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM experiments, including learning curves under full-state and visual observations with dense and sparse rewards.

after.justification: v2 retains original PPO experiments and adds SAC, TD-MPC2, offline RL, and VLA evaluations in Sections 6.2–6.4, Tables 4 and 6, and Appendix F.

M1.justification: The four memory categories, two-tier MIKASA-Base design, and MIKASA-Robo task procedures and reward structures are retained. The additions evaluate existing agent families and supply demonstration datasets; they do not introduce a new proposed learning algorithm or memory component.

E1.justification: v2 adds expert-demonstration datasets actually used for offline training across all 32 robotic tasks, plus language-paired demonstrations for five VLA tasks (Appendices B and D). These training datasets are absent from v1's online experiments. The underlying robotic tasks and MIKASA-Base environment inventory remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM, v2 evaluates SAC-MLP and TD-MPC2 in selected dense-reward comparisons, RATE, DT, BC, CQL, and Diffusion Policy across all 32 offline tasks, and Octo-small and OpenVLA on five tasks. Participation is documented in Figures 5 and 9 and Tables 4 and 6.

E3.justification: v2 introduces RGB-only offline training with sparse rewards and 1,000 successful trajectories per task. VLA experiments use 250 demonstrations, 50,000 training iterations, end-effector control, and specified context and action-chunk settings. Revised online plots also change displayed training horizons and label some ordinates Return instead of Success Rate; whether this reflects a metric change or relabeling is unclear.

E4.justification: v2 Table 4 adds an OpenVLA action-chunk sensitivity comparison, K=4 versus K=8, across five tasks, examining whether chunking compensates for missing observation history. The existing observation-mode, reward-density, architecture, and task-difficulty analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports mean ± SEM from three training runs with 16 evaluation seeds; v2 retains this description in Appendix F. v2 additionally specifies 100-episode VLA evaluation, three runs with 100 episodes per run for offline results, and seeds 1–100 in Appendix G. The general 100-episode description is not reconciled with the retained 16-seed account, so an across-the-board rerun cannot be established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial online, offline, and VLA results. Table 6 reports RATE at 0.92±0.01 on ShellGameTouch and Diffusion Policy at 0.68±0.02 on InterceptMedium; all five offline methods report zero success on the nine capacity/sequential tasks. Table 4 reports OpenVLA RememberColor3 success of 0.21±0.00 for K=4 and 0.59±0.04 for K=8. These are new comparisons, while the original PPO oracle-solvability findings remain.

T1.justification: The POMDP definition, expected-return objective, correlation-horizon condition, and mathematics in the retained task descriptions are unchanged. Neither version adds original theorems or proofs relative to the other.

C1.justification: v1 presents three main contributions: the taxonomy, MIKASA-Base, and MIKASA-Robo. v2's introduction and conclusion add released offline datasets as a fourth contribution and broaden the empirical conclusions to online, offline, and VLA agents. The original three contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds action chunking as a possible memory shortcut and interprets limitations of SAC, TD-MPC2, and VLA agents. Its new limitations section qualifies VLA conclusions because fine-tuning was computationally constrained and identifies longer dependencies and meta-RL as remaining extensions. Table 1 also changes RotateStrict's memory classification from Object to Spatial.

D1.justification: v2 adds package installation instructions and updated examples, dataset schemas and collection procedures, reported access to PPO checkpoints and collection scripts, VLA controller and fine-tuning specifications, and single-NVIDIA-A100 hardware information (Appendices A, B, D, and G). These substantially extend v1's environment examples and task documentation.

R1.justification: v1 says no dedicated robotic-manipulation memory benchmark is known. v2 acknowledges concurrent MemoryBench and positions MIKASA-Robo through broader memory categories, task coverage, and efficient parallelization (Sections 2 and 6). It also adds FetchBench to Table 3 and references supporting the expanded offline RL and VLA evaluations.

P1.justification: Substantial rewrites affect the MIKASA-Base motivation and design narrative, related-work discussion, contribution list, and conclusion. Section 6 is reorganized around online, offline, and VLA evaluations; concrete robotic examples and a standalone limitations section are added. The detailed task appendices remain largely verbatim despite renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adds radar Figure 6 and VLA, instruction, and offline-results Tables 4–6, expands selected learning curves with additional baselines, and redraws the sparse-reward plots. v1's recommended-task Table 4 is removed. Typography, table coloring, and figure placement also change, while the appendix task illustrations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation beyond v1's two PPO backbones through diverse online, offline, and VLA evaluations. Documented demonstration datasets expand the benchmark's practical usefulness, while action-chunk sensitivity tests and explicit fine-tuning limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: the 16-seed and 100-episode descriptions remain unreconciled, and revised plots mix Return and Success Rate labels, limiting precise comparisons.
